profiles.text:
Overview

   This chapter begins with a practical mathematical question. Once a family of operators has been
fixed, what can we generate from a few starting vectors, and how can we keep track of the resulting
object? The answer has two parts. Seed rank measures how many starting vectors are needed. Packet
coordinates describe the components of vectors and the transfers between them.
   The construction starts with a typed operator grammar and a concrete realization of that gram-
mar. From there we study generated hulls, presentations by seeds and relations, and the number of
generators required by a module. The generator results include reduction modulo the Jacobson rad-
ical, the semisimple multiplicity formula over division rings, and the formula for a single operator
over an arbitrary field.
  We then resolve vectors and operators using complete families of idempotents. Finite packet re-
construction is exact. Countable reconstruction requires the stated convergence assumptions. Trans-
fer blocks record the action from each input packet to each output packet, and their multiplication
exposes both admissible paths and cancellation. Later sections develop quotient descent, coordinate
changes, completion, and transport through realization functors.
   Worked quiver, coordinate ring, matrix, graph, and shift models show how the same language
is used in different settings. The visual atlas follows these models through complete calculations.
Stable statement identifiers connect this text to the existing machine companion, while the sepa-
rate Lean guide specifies the scope of the formal certificates. The written proofs and the imported
classical results retain their stated hypotheses.

Reader’s orientation


  Status class                       Meaning

  Definition                             Introduced structure or notation.
  Theorem, proposition, corollary, lemma  Proved in this manuscript under the printed
                                         hypotheses.
  Classical input                       Imported standard theorem, stated explicitly because
                                                  later proofs depend on it.
  Boundary                  A limitation, counterexample, or failure of an
                                           implication that is part of the formal scope.


Formal and computational companions. The formal companion explains the Lean development, its
build procedure, theorem mapping, and the hypotheses of each verified statement. It distinguishes the
35-row foundational contract from the correspondence for the 108-record mathematical inventory. The
computational companion presents those stable records, dependencies, and executable interfaces. Both
companions are collected in the back matter. The mathematics below retains the full scope of its stated
classical inputs and written proofs.


  A route through this section

  The argument has four stages. Reading them in order makes the later examples easier to follow.

     1. Grammar and realization. Specify which compositions of operators are legal, then distinguish
       that abstract syntax from the operators that actually act on a chosen space.

     2. Generation. Choose one or more seeds and ask which part of the realization is generated by
       their operator orbits. The minimal number of required seeds is the seed rank.

     3. Packet coordinates. Resolve the space by a complete family of idempotents. Every vector and
      every operator then has exact packet coordinates.

     4. Transport. Study how those coordinates behave under products, graphs, morphisms, quo-
        tients, completion, and realization functors.

  The first two layers describe what can be generated. The last two describe how the generated object
   is resolved and transported.



The basic conceptual chain

                      typed grammar ⟶realized algebra ⟶seed hull

                   ⟶seed rank ⟶packet coordinates

                      ⟶transfer blocks ⟶functorial realization.


  Each object in this chain has a different role. A grammar is a presentation of allowed operator words.
A realized algebra is the image of that grammar in an endomorphism algebra. A seed hull is an orbit
span inside one particular module. A packet system is an exact coordinate decomposition and need
not be orthogonal. A realization functor is required to preserve a declared mathematical profile, not
merely the vocabulary.

Computational records and interfaces

This computational companion represents Chapter I as a collection of mathematical records that can be
inspected and queried, with a finite subset supported by executable interfaces. The statement inventory
is formal/coverage/COVERAGE_108.json. The executable runtime has its own entrypoint under
source/machine_v1.0.1/. That path identifies the exact archived payload. The catalogue and runtime
have the distinct scopes explained below.

  The catalogue contains 108 mathematical records, including 69 theorem, proposition, corollary, and
lemma records with source proofs. The formal correspondence is reported alongside each record. The
preserved runtime interface has twenty typed signatures, and its attached historical Lean tranche has
eight mappings. Those inherited interfaces and receipts retain their original scope.

  The mathematical source supplies the statements and proofs, including the split-semisimple hypothe-
ses and explicit map qualifications. The supplementary worked models remain in the mathematical
text. Stable identifiers connect the mathematical, formal, and computational material. Statement hashes
and source locators distinguish the catalogue from the archived runtime payloads.

  The verification record distinguishes evidence for the mathematical correspondence from the runtime
receipts. Its source inventory and formal correspondence map are available under formal/coverage/,
and compiler and replay receipts are under formal/evidence/. The Lean guide explains the formal
sources, their hypotheses, and how to interpret those checks.

 How to use this volume. Read Sections 1–3 for mathematical and evidence semantics. Sections 4–6
give the executable contracts and an exact worked example. Section 7 describes reproduction. Appendix
A reproduces every canonical source statement and every attached proof body, with source locators
and machine metadata. Later appendices give signatures, action coverage, operation vocabulary, and
the historical Lean map.

1 The mathematical object behind the interface

1.1 Operator systems, generated hulls, and seed rank

A seed problem consists of an acting algebra, a module, and a family of seed vectors. The algebra must
be fixed before the generation question is asked. For a unital algebra A acting on a module M and a
finite seed family S = {s1, . . . , sr}, the algebraic generated hull is

                                                                                    r
                                   HullA(S) = ∑ Asj.
                                                           j=1

A one-seed system is cyclic. Seed rank measures the minimum cardinality of a generating family,
under the regime declared in the source. Enlarging the acting algebra changes the question. Replacing
algebraic span by a closure changes it again. The machine record therefore keeps the acting regime and
hypotheses beside the statement.

  Chapter I begins with typed operator grammars and their realizations, then passes through free
presentations, generator number, packet coordinates, block algebras, transfer graphs, and realization.
The resulting record graph covers the whole expanded foundation. It is not limited to the finite matrix
examples that the runtime executes.
  For finite families of nonnegative integers, the ambient convention is max ∅= 0. The height of an
empty finite poset is zero. A nonempty poset with no strict comparable pair also has height zero, so
height counts strict steps. These conventions clarify the empty cases without adding stable records.

  The source separates algebraic, linear, and topological claims. A finite-dimensional matrix computa-
tion can exercise a linear identity. It cannot establish the Banach space result in the countable setting
or a generator formula over every division ring. Those claims retain their own source proofs and
dependencies.


1.2 Exact packet coordinates

For a finite index set I, a packet system on X consists of linear maps Pα satisfying

                       P2α = Pα,     PβPα = 0  (β ̸= α),  ∑ Pα = IX.
                                                                      α∈I

The packet spaces are the ranges Xα = PαX. Analysis and synthesis are

                     APx = (Pαx)α∈I,     SP((xα)α) = ∑ xα.
                                                                           α

Their inverse laws are exact. No assumption of inner product orthogonality is needed. This distinction
is visible in the oblique two-dimensional example later in this companion.

  Machine execution represents each packet as an ambient vector. It does not construct a basis of every
range or replace the ambient representation by smaller coordinate arrays. This choice makes exact
identities easy to compare with the source formulas while retaining the packet index structure.

1.3 Transfer blocks and composition

For an endomorphism T, the transfer block from packet α to packet β is

                                          Tβα = PβTPα.

Its source is Xα and its target is Xβ. In the finite runtime it is stored as a full ambient matrix. Complete-
ness gives
                       T = ∑ Tβα,    (ST)γα = ∑ SγβTβα.
                                                 α,β                      β

The order matters: the rightmost factor acts first. The runtime uses the same convention. Its nested
block array is indexed first by target and then by source.

  The graph records source dependencies for these identities. It does not infer every implicit math-
ematical dependency. The packet-system hypotheses remain required even when a compact source
statement inherits them from the surrounding section.


1.4 Intertwining and reconstruction

For packet systems P on X and Q on Y, an intertwiner U : X →Y satisfies UT = SU. Resolving both
sides yields
            ∑ UγβTβα = ∑ SγδUδα,    Uγα = QγUPα.
                                 β                δ

All local equations together are equivalent to the global equation under the packet hypotheses. The
runtime returns the global Boolean, every local residual, and the conjunction of the local Booleans. It
provides the data needed to inspect agreement or failure in a concrete exact case.


1.5 The boundary of finite execution

Countable packet sums require a topology and a convergence condition. Quotient descent requires
invariance. Coordinate transport requires a suitable invertible map. Packet-pure seed counts differ from
unrestricted seed counts because one mixed-support seed can contribute to several source components.
These are mathematical hypotheses, not formatting conventions.

  The source records seven explicit boundaries. Their presence is part of the interface. Runtime action
names do not imply that every associated theorem has an implementation, and metadata listing a
boundary does not itself execute that boundary check.


2 Canonical machine representation

2.1 Entrypoint and package identity

The mathematical records are located at formal/coverage/COVERAGE_108.json. Appendix A is
generated directly from those records. Each includes the statement, source proof where present, source
location, hashes, formal status, and declaration correspondence. The archived mathematical source
identified by those hashes is the statement authority.

  The preserved executable payload is located at source/machine_v1.0.1/. Runtime commands
in this volume assume that working directory. Its entrypoint, PSC_I.machine.json, points to the
preserved record collection, statement AST, dependency graph, action registry, and evidence index. A

profiles.text:
1 Reading the mathematical, formal, and computational texts together

The mathematical text develops the language and its examples. The computational companion gives
stable records, typed dependencies, semantic profiles, and executable validation interfaces. This guide
makes the Lean development usable: where the definitions live, what each theorem actually accepts,
how its proof works, and what evidence connects the delivered source to an accepted kernel run.

  The foundational formalization taught in Sections 3–14 is the 20-file project preserved at source/t
raditional_v1.3.1/formalization/lean/ in the source archive. The path identifies that exact archived
component. The mathematical text contains an expanded core with 108 stable records. Those records
form a different inventory from the 35 Lean contract rows.

  The guide retains both the scope and the exclusions of every contract row. For example, historical
row 10 proves a split-semisimple formula after algebra and module equivalences are supplied. The later
continuation constructs compatible decompositions and establishes the general division-ring formula.
The new result is documented through its own declarations and evidence. It does not change the inputs
of historical row 10.


1.1 What the numbers count


 Quantity        Meaning

 20 source files     Local Lean files, including the import aggregator, focused Mathlib import file,
                and standalone audit.
 35 contract rows   Mathematical statement families and specifications in the foundational con-
                       tract map.
 84 mapped  tar-  Distinct Lean declaration names used by those rows. They include definitions
 gets            and equivalences as well as theorems.
 1,126 entries       Entries in the project namespace inspected by the historical audit, including
                   generated helpers.
 108        stable  The expanded manuscript inventory. The current correspondence map and
 records            the machine payload’s historical eight-record map have different evidence
                     scopes.

  None of these figures is a count of 1,126 independent new theorems. The useful unit of mathematical
coverage is a statement together with its hypotheses, its precise conclusion, its declaration target, and
the evidence attached to that target.


1.2 Suggested reading routes

A reader new to Lean can begin with Sections 3–5, which unpack the syntax through exact packet
coordinates. A mathematician checking coverage can go directly to the exhaustive map in Section 14,
then inspect the relevant source type and proof. A contributor preparing a build should read Sections 10
and 11 before interpreting any successful command.

  The displayed Lean listings are excerpts from the preserved source. Their surrounding imports,
namespace declarations, and section variables remain in the original files. They are reading excerpts,
not advertised standalone files. The editable companion includes their source ranges and hashes in
generated/excerpts.json.

2 Formal sources, correspondence, and evidence

The mathematical text and both companions share one statement inventory. The traditional manuscript
supplies the statements and proofs. The machine catalog reproduces those statements with stable iden-
tifiers and source locators. The formal correspondence map records the exact Lean support for each
statement. The source archive uses the following stable paths:


    File or directory                      Purpose

   formal/current/                            Flat formal source closure, including the continuation mod-
                                              ules and their earlier dependencies.
   formal/coverage/COVERAGE_108.json      All 108 statements, source proofs and hashes, declaration
                                        mappings, scopes, and record classifications.
   formal/evidence/                       Compiler, replay, audit, identity, and boundary-check receipts,
                                         indexed by the verification record.
   editable/traditional/                 Mathematical source, including the stated hypotheses of the
                                             split-semisimple corollary.
   source/traditional_v1.3.1/             Source and evidence for the 35-row foundational contract.


  The inventory has 69 proof-level records. Definitions, classical inputs, boundaries, and documentary
records are listed separately in the map and are excluded from this proof-level count.


                        Status             Covered   Partial  Not mapped

                        Proof-level records        69       0            0


  “Covered” means a complete correspondence at the recorded scope. “Partial” includes substantive
missing proofs and consequences not yet assembled from existing declarations. “Not mapped” means
that this source closure has no established complete declaration for the record. These statuses are not
a percentage of independent theorems: the records differ in scope and may share mathematical depen-
dencies.


2.1 Primary and semisimple constructions

The verification receipt for the primary and semisimple constructions (archival identifier Block 08)
covers 54 production modules. It freshly compiled eight additions, authenticated 46 predecessor
source/object pairs, and replayed the whole logical closure. Its 1,634 source-owned entries comprise
1,627 logical declarations and seven separately inventoried generated partial runtime helpers. The lat-
ter were not proof-replayed. The recorded transitive axiom set is limited to propext, Classical.choice,
and Quot.sound. These quantities describe that receipt. It does not claim that all 54 source modules
were freshly compiled.

  The continuation proves the intrinsic primary quotient and generator count, the geometric for-
mula, scalar extension, and the six-way cyclic criterion. It also proves noncommutative module-top
reduction and the nonsplit semisimple formula, including actual compatible decompositions from the
Wedderburn–Artin existence theorem. The final existence theorems do not take a desired rank equality
or a compatible decomposition as an input. They are noncomputable mathematical constructions, not
executable decomposition algorithms.

REALIZATION CALCULUS




CHAPTER II

Projector Resolved Seed Calculus II

Refinement towers, weighted transfer, and integral separation of
operator packets





An exact account of how packet coordinates refine, weighted transfers accumulate, and rational

splittings become visible on an integral lattice.





Komorebi P.


Mathematical text

profiles.text:
How to use this volume

  Reading route. Exact packet coordinates and residue selectors lead to weighted inversion and
   rational walk series. Lattice gluing then gives separation weights and precision delays. Smith con-
  gruences and operator defects connect these formulas to finite computation.

  Companions. The worked plates illustrate the constructions of this chapter. The formal companion
   in the back matter distinguishes the chapter-wide correspondence from the foundational 25-row
  walkthrough, with explicit evidence and scope.



                                       Overview

     A complete family of idempotents gives exact coordinates, but a single family does not record
      scale or integral visibility. We study towers in which every coarse idempotent is the sum of its fine
      descendants. The coordinate changes are invertible and coherent, and every operator block is the
    sum of its refined blocks. Residue selectors give a model over arbitrary rings. When roots of unity
      are available they agree with character averages, and coprime moduli factor through the Chinese re-
     mainder theorem. In a complete filtered algebra, a diagonal operator plus positive weight transfers
      has an inverse obtained by summing admissible weighted paths. The formula truncates exactly at
       finite precision, while finite transfer graphs have rational path series. For a rational spectral decom-
      position over a discrete valuation ring, resultants give denominator bounds. The exact denominator
        is the largest Smith exponent of the lattice gluing module. This yields a necessary and sufficient pre-
      cision delay, monotonicity under refinement, and a full congruence solving formula. We close with
      exact formulas for the propagation of a coarsening defect through powers, resolvents, holomorphic
      functions, exponentials, and multilevel towers.

The exposition distinguishes general written proofs, formal specifications, and finite computational
examples. The worked plates supply concrete models. The formal companion identifies the exact dec-
larations and hypotheses that support each mapped statement.

1 Introduction

A complete family of pairwise annihilating idempotents decomposes a module into exact coordinate
pieces. Many problems require more than one such decomposition. A signal may be split first into
two residue classes and then into four. A filtered operator may be resolved into transfers that appear at
different valuation depths. A rational spectral splitting may exist over the fraction field while remaining
invisible on the original lattice. These are all refinement problems, but they involve different notions
of scale.

  The first part of the chapter concerns exact refinement. If a fine packet family refines a coarse family,
then each coarse idempotent is the sum of its fine descendants. The coordinate spaces at the two levels
are canonically isomorphic because both represent the whole module. The refinement relation adds
more information. It tells us which fine coordinates belong to each coarse coordinate, and it gives a
compatible decomposition of every operator block. This is the algebra behind polyphase coordinates
and nested filter banks. Standard treatments of those subjects may be found in [10, 2].

  The second part studies inversion in a complete filtered algebra. Suppose an operator has the form

                      𝑇= 𝐷+ 𝑁,

where 𝐷is invertible and every packet transfer in 𝑁raises the filtration by a positive amount. The
ordinary Neumann series can then be expanded into weighted paths. The weight is not the number
of edges. It is the total filtration gain along the path. At precision 𝐿, every path of weight at least 𝐿
vanishes. A finite transfer graph also gives a rational generating function for the number of paths of
each total weight. The relevant generating function facts are classical and are discussed in [9].
  The third part concerns integral separation. Let 𝑉be a vector space over the fraction field of a discrete
valuation ring 𝒪, and let Λ be an 𝒪lattice in 𝑉. A rational projector 𝐸need not preserve Λ. Its separation
weight is the least 𝑠such that
                                𝜋𝑠𝐸Λ ⊆Λ.

A Bézout construction gives an upper bound through a polynomial resultant. That bound need not
be exact because it does not see the position of the lattice. The exact answer is controlled by the finite
length module
                          𝐺Λ,𝒫= Λ/ ⨁ (Λ ∩𝑉𝛼),
                                            𝛼
where 𝑉= ⨁𝛼𝑉𝛼is the rational packet decomposition. The largest Smith exponent of this gluing
module is exactly the common denominator needed to make every packet projector integral. This in-
terpretation also proves that separation weight cannot decrease under refinement. Background on local
fields, Smith normal form, and matrix polynomials may be found in [8, 6, 3].

  The last part records how a defect between fine and coarse operators propagates. If

                      Δ = 𝐶𝑇𝑓−𝑇𝑐𝐶,

then exact formulas describe the corresponding defect for powers, resolvents, holomorphic functions,
exponentials, and a chain of several refinement levels. These formulas are elementary, but collecting
them in one place makes the later analytic uses transparent. The spectral and resolvent background
follows the usual operator theory in [4].

Every theorem in this chapter concerns linear operators. An exact refinement retains the full object
and changes its coordinates. Questions about nonlinear operation trees, nonlinear correction, and ob-
struction complexes require a separate theory.


2 Depth and compatibility

Packet, filtration, and separation depths describe three different kinds of scale. Compatibility is initially
recorded by an operator defect. Keeping these notions separate makes the later formulas easier to read.

  The first is packet depth. A finer packet family has more idempotents and a more detailed address
set. The passage from residues modulo two to residues modulo four is an example. Packet depth is
combinatorial. It says how many distinctions have been made in the coordinate system.
  The second is filtration depth. A transfer in 𝐹𝑟ℬvanishes modulo 𝐹𝑟ℬ. This membership gives a
lower bound on its depth. A nonzero transfer may first become visible only at a higher precision. Two
paths with the same number of edges can have different filtration depths. A longer path can appear
earlier when its edges have smaller weights.
  The third is separation depth. A rational packet projector may require multiplication by 𝜋𝑠before it
preserves the chosen lattice. This number depends on both the rational decomposition and the lattice.
It can be zero even when the corresponding eigenvalues are close, and it can be positive even when the
rational projector is simple.

  The fourth notion is the compatibility defect. A fine operator and a separately chosen coarse operator
need not commute with coarsening. Their discrepancy is

                      Δ = 𝐶𝑇𝑓−𝑇𝑐𝐶.

This operator records the failure of one model to represent another exactly. A chosen norm measures
its size, while a chosen filtration can assign a depth. No integer compatibility depth is assigned without
that additional structure.

  The four notions meet in applications, but no one of them determines the others. An exact refinement
tower may have zero coordinate error while its fine spectral packets have positive lattice weight. A
filtered inverse may truncate exactly at a given depth while the coarse operator still has a nonzero
compatibility defect. The chapter treats each quantity with its own theorem before combining them.


  The central idea

   Packet depth changes the address of a component. Filtration depth controls when a transfer sur-
   vives a precision cutoff. Separation depth clears a rational denominator on a chosen lattice. The
   compatibility defect records a discrepancy between two operator models. These quantities can
   interact, but each needs its own hypothesis and its own calculation.

How to use this volume
Reading route. Exact packet coordinates and residue selectors lead to weighted inversion and
rational walk series. Lattice gluing then gives separation weights and precision delays. Smith con-
gruences and operator defects connect these formulas to finite computation.
Companions. The worked plates illustrate the constructions of this chapter. The formal companion
in the back matter distinguishes the chapter-wide correspondence from the foundational 25-row
walkthrough, with explicit evidence and scope.
Overview
A complete family of idempotents gives exact coordinates, but a single family does not record
scale or integral visibility. We study towers in which every coarse idempotent is the sum of its fine
descendants. The coordinate changes are invertible and coherent, and every operator block is the
sum of its refined blocks. Residue selectors give a model over arbitrary rings. When roots of unity
are available they agree with character averages, and coprime moduli factor through the Chinese re-
mainder theorem. In a complete filtered algebra, a diagonal operator plus positive weight transfers
has an inverse obtained by summing admissible weighted paths. The formula truncates exactly at
finite precision, while finite transfer graphs have rational path series. For a rational spectral decom-
position over a discrete valuation ring, resultants give denominator bounds. The exact denominator
is the largest Smith exponent of the lattice gluing module. This yields a necessary and sufficient pre-
cision delay, monotonicity under refinement, and a full congruence solving formula. We close with
exact formulas for the propagation of a coarsening defect through powers, resolvents, holomorphic
functions, exponentials, and multilevel towers.
The exposition distinguishes general written proofs, formal specifications, and finite computational
examples. The worked plates supply concrete models. The formal companion identifies the exact dec-
larations and hypotheses that support each mapped statement.

Plate II.1    / CHAPTER II / A WORKED VISUAL GUIDE

 Three kinds of resolution

   Chapter II, mathematical text: Definition 3.4, Theorem 5.10, Theorem 7.7

  Chapter II asks three different questions that can all sound like “increase the resolution.” This guide separates
them, then follows small objects far enough that the distinctions can be computed rather than merely named.

      ADDRESS            WEIGHT            SEPARATION


                                                                         1
     0    2    4    6           𝑎𝑏𝑎     4               1    2
                                  𝑏    2                    0   0
     0    4    2    6                          𝑎   1

                                                2𝐸+ integral
  4 coordinates at both levels    𝑊(𝑎𝑏𝑎) = 1 + 2 + 1 = 4
                                             𝐸+ not integral

Three different operations. On the left, all coefficients survive a regrouping. In the middle, an integer weight controls which
operator words can matter modulo a chosen power. On the right, a rational projector needs a denominator cleared before
integral precision can be recovered.

  Address resolution
 A coefficient such as 𝑥6 can sit in the even packet, then the residue-2 packet modulo 4, then the residue-6
packet modulo 8. Its value does not become more accurate. Its address becomes more specific, while the full object
remains exactly reconstructible.

  Arithmetic precision

  An operator word with total filtration weight at least 𝐿vanishes in the specified depth-𝐿quotient. Increasing 𝐿
can make additional words relevant. This is a change in the precision of the ring in which the answer is required,
not a lossless rearrangement of one fixed list.

  Separation precision
  For the integral involution used later, 𝐸+ = (𝐼+ 𝐴)/2 is an exact rational projector but not an integral one at 2.
One extra input digit suffices to recover the projected difference to the requested precision. The packet is present
over the fraction field even when its integral separation is delayed.

  Read this as: Keep three quantities distinct: the packet address, the precision cutoff, and the denominator
   weight. Finer addresses do not automatically improve arithmetic precision or remove a spectral denomi-
   nator.

Plate II.3    / MODEL A / LOSSLESS ADDRESS REFINEMENT

 Follow one coefficient through the tower

   Chapter II, mathematical text: Theorem 3.3, Theorem 4.6

  Take a vector 𝑥= (𝑥0, … , 𝑥15). A packet is not a single summary number: it retains every coefficient at its
selected addresses. For example,
                                𝑃2,0𝑥= (𝑥0, 0, 𝑥2, 0, … , 𝑥14, 0).

The rail below lists the addresses in each packet. Its display order groups descendants under their parents. The
matrix example on Plate II.5 instead uses increasing residue order.

                   𝑟= 0                       𝑟= 1

 𝑁= 2    0   2   4   6   8   10  12  14   1   3   5   7   9   11  13  15    16


             𝑟= 0          𝑟= 2          𝑟= 1          𝑟= 3

 𝑁= 4    0   4   8   12   2   6   10  14   1   5   9   13   3   7   11  15    16


         𝑟= 0   𝑟= 4   𝑟= 2   𝑟= 6   𝑟= 1   𝑟= 5   𝑟= 3   𝑟= 7

 𝑁= 8    0   8   4   12   2   10   6   14   1   9   5   13   3   11   7   15    16


                   Each cell is an address n; its coefficient travels with it.

Every row contains all sixteen addresses exactly once. A heavier boundary separates packet ranges. The numbers are coeffi-
cient addresses, not new coefficient values. There is no interpolation, averaging, or omitted high-frequency tail.
  The address 6 is even, is 2 modulo 4, and is 6 modulo 8. Its coefficient therefore lies in the successive ranges

                                𝑃8,6𝑋⊆𝑃4,2𝑋⊆𝑃2,0𝑋.

The corresponding identities hold as operators:

                                     𝑃2,0 = 𝑃4,0 + 𝑃4,2,     𝑃4,2 = 𝑃8,2 + 𝑃8,6.

Applying either composite parent selector to 𝑃8,6𝑥leaves it unchanged. Applying the odd selector kills it. This
is absorption between a parent and a child, rather than an approximate resemblance between nearby scales.

  Why the reconstruction is unique

    If a vector is a sum of components in disjoint packet ranges, apply the projector for one range. All other com-
ponents vanish and the selected component remains. Thus every child component is recovered uniquely from
the sum.

  Read this as: Refinement is a sharper address book for the same coefficients. The total number of free
   coordinates does not change.

 Regrouping is not averaging

   Chapter II, mathematical text: Definition 3.4, Theorem 3.5

  The word coarsening can suggest compression. In the exact coordinate theorem it means regrouping complete
packet vectors. Replacing each packet by one scalar sum is a different operation and really does lose information.
  For 𝑥= (1, 2, 3, 4), the fine packets are the four coordinate-supported vectors. Regrouping gives (1, 0, 3, 0) and
(0, 2, 0, 4). Every original coordinate remains available in one of these two vectors.

     Fine packet vectors     Coarse packet vectors         Scalar incidence only

       1  0  0  0            1  0  3  0               1  0  1  0

       0  2  0  0            0  2  0  4               0  1  0  1
                         ∑children       0  0  3  0
                                                           (𝑥0 + 𝑥2, 𝑥1 + 𝑥3)       0  0  0  4



 4 × 1 = 4 free coordinates 2 × 2 = 4 free coordinates       4 ⟶2 scalars: loss


The left and middle panels store the same four independent coordinates. The right panel instead applies a 2 × 4 numerical
incidence matrix to four scalar entries. That is not the range-restricted exact coordinate map.

  Define
                      𝑋pkt𝑁= ⨁ 𝑃𝑁,𝑗𝑋,   𝒜𝑁𝑥= (𝑃𝑁,𝑗𝑥)𝑗,    𝒮𝑁(𝑥𝑗)𝑗= ∑ 𝑥𝑗.
                                            𝑗                                                                𝑗

Completeness and mutual annihilation give both inverse laws. Consequently,

                𝐽= 𝒜4𝒮2,  𝐶= 𝒜2𝒮4,   𝐶𝐽= 𝐼, 𝐽𝐶= 𝐼.

The larger list of fine packets has smaller individual packet spaces.

  A kernel witnesses genuine information loss

  For the scalar incidence matrix 𝐵drawn on the right,

                                          𝐵(1, 0, −1, 0)T = 0.

The zero vector and (1, 0, −1, 0) therefore have the same two scalar summaries. No inverse can recover the original
four scalars from that output alone.

The Lean project is formal/current/. Its correspondence records the exact statement and proof text,
source hashes, fully qualified targets, and the evidence attached to each item. The complete machine-
readable record is formal/coverage/Paper_II_Current_Correspondence_2026-10-19.json.

  Formal correspondence. The correspondence records 81 source items, including 53 proof-level items.
Its status is FINAL_SOURCE_BOUND_CORRESPONDENCE_53_OF_53. The tables retain the recorded states and
verification checks. The inherited 25-row map remains a separate historical contract.

  53 of 53 proof-level source records have kernel checked, semantically accepted scope. No partial or
pending proof records are listed in this correspondence. These are source-record counts under their
stated hypotheses, not counts of independent discoveries.

Part I  Finite typed transfer and the formal contract


The finite algebraic core supplies the algebraic foundation and a contract for its individual declarations.
Here, “roadmap” and “outside the contract” describe the scope of the finite Lean formalization. Ordi-
nary mathematical results in Part II may lie beyond that scope. The finite contract covers thirty result
environments. The source contract has 41 mapping rows because it also includes definitions and other
interfaces.

The formal companion records the exact Lean and Mathlib dependencies [3, 17], compilation, kernel
replay, and axiom checks. References to declarations from Chapters I–II retain their explicitly inherited
status. The companion distinguishes the finite algebraic contract from the additional packet-coordinate
and analytic interfaces.


1 Purpose and formal status

Chapter I fixed typed seeds, operator grammars, exact projector packets, generated hulls, and recon-
struction [13]. Chapter II added coherent refinement coordinates, weighted transfer, arithmetic sepa-
ration, and linear defect identities [14]. The present chapter begins the next layer: explicit edge words,
optional connection data, and obstructions within individual packets.

  Canonical coordinate transport and a connection play different mathematical roles. Canonical trans-
port compares two exact descriptions of the same ambient object and is forced by analysis and synthesis.
A connection chooses transports that may carry extra modeling, discretization, or gauge information.
Canonical transport obeys a cocycle theorem. A connection may fail to obey a cocycle, and that fail-
ure is meaningful data. Keeping separate notation lets us distinguish the automatic coherence of exact
coordinates from the possible holonomy of a chosen connection.


1.1 Statement labels

Every substantial theorem, lemma, corollary, proposition, definition, API, and roadmap item carries
one or more of the three labels below. When separate clauses use a Chapter III result and an inherited
bridge, the statement carries both applicable labels. Illustrative examples do not require a label.

   S1. Lean-backed in Chapter III: the displayed scope is no stronger than the named compiled dec-
        laration in the identified Chapter III module.

   S2. Inherited Lean-backed: the displayed result is supplied by the frozen formal contract of Chap-
        ter I or Chapter II.

   S3. Roadmap only: the text states a future interface or theorem target and is excluded from the
       completion denominator.

Boundary 1.1 (Finite theorem denominator). The completion denominator of the finite algebraic con-
tract consists of the thirty result environments in Part I. Of these, 26 resolve to compiled Chapter III dec-
larations and four resolve to the frozen Chapters I–II contracts. The authoritative theorem map names
the exact declarations used by each statement. The kernel audit checks those targets and their sup-
porting theorems. The namespace gate requires every declaration in the compiled Komorebi.PaperIII

REALIZATION CALCULUS
               Projector Resolved Seed Calculus III
      Analytic Packet Jets and Exact Composition

                       Mathematical and verification supplement

                                     Komorebi P.



This supplement gives full ordinary mathematical arguments for the analytic packet claims of Section

17, identifies a stronger norm bound, and records how the calculation relates to the actual projector
ranges. The accompanying formal development verifies multilinear reconstruction, continuous jets on the
actual projector ranges, their norm bound, and the decorated composition and structural support laws.
The ordinary Taylor and counting arguments retain their proof status as stated here. The companion
Lean guide identifies the exact declarations and replay evidence.


1 Two distinct contracts

Let X, Y, Z be real Banach spaces. The same statements hold for complex Banach spaces with complex
Fréchet derivatives. The integral below uses a real parameter. A bounded packet system on X is a finite
family Pi ∈L(X, X) such that

         X Pi = idX,   Pi2 = Pi,     PiPj = 0   (i ̸= j).                        (1)
                               i∈I

Write Xi = ran Pi with the subspace norm. Analogously, let (Qγ)γ∈J and (Rδ)δ∈K be bounded packet
systems on Y and Z. Zero projectors are allowed in this supplement. An empty family can satisfy (1)
only on the zero space. Its coordinate product is the zero vector space with norm zero. For a continuous
r-linear map, the operator norm is the supremum over tuples whose individual norms are at most
one. Derivative orders are nonnegative integers, and a packet jet has positive order unless a nullary
convention is explicitly invoked.
  A weaker family of operators that only satisfies Pi Pi = id yields a useful algebraic expansion, but it
need not produce independent coordinates. We keep these statements separate.

Lemma 1.1 (Closed ranges and bounded coordinates). Each Xi is closed. The maps

                   AX(x) = (Pix)i∈I : X −→ Y Xi,     SX((zi)i∈I) = X zi
                                                         i∈I                          i∈I

are inverse bounded linear maps when the finite product carries the maximum norm.

Proof. The identity ran Pi = ker(id −Pi) follows from idempotence. The kernel of a continuous linear
map is closed, so each range is itself Banach. Both coordinate maps are bounded because the family is
finite. The identity Pi Pi = idX gives SXAX = id. If zi ∈ran Pi, then Pizi = zi and Pjzi = 0 for j ̸= i.
Thus AXSX = id. Moreover, ∥AX∥≤maxi ∥Pi∥and ∥SX∥≤|I| whenever I is nonempty. The case of
the zero space follows from the identities directly.

2 Multilinear reconstruction and packet jets

Theorem 2.1 (Completeness is enough for multilinear expansion). Let I, J be finite and r ≥0. Suppose
Pi Pi = idX and Pγ Qγ = idY, without assuming idempotence or annihilation. Let B  : Xr →Y be
multilinear. Then, for all h1, . . . , hr ∈X,

                        B(h1, . . . , hr) = X X QγB(Pα1h1, . . . , Pαrhr).                         (2)
                                         γ∈J α∈Ir

The statement includes r = 0 under the usual empty-product convention.

Proof. For every input, ha = Pi∈I Piha. Additivity in each slot expands B into the sum over all choices
α ∈Ir. The finite output identity expresses each resulting value as its sum of Qγ components. All
exchanges of sums are finite. No property beyond completeness and multilinearity enters the calculation.
For r = 0, the sum over input indices has exactly one term, and output completeness still gives the
identity.

B : Xr →Y be a continuous multilinear map, r ≥1. The formula

Let U ⊂X be open and F  : U →Y be Cm. For 1 ≤r ≤m, the Fréchet derivative DrF(x) is a continuous
multilinear map. Apply Theorem 2.1 to B = DrF(x). Thus the actual packet jets recover the entire
derivative, without presupposing a separate packet derivative object.

Corollary 3.1 (Conjugated derivatives in packet coordinates). Let bF = AY ◦F ◦SX on the open set
AX(U). Then bF is Cm and, for 1 ≤r ≤m,

The operators AY and SX are bounded and linear. Their derivatives of order at least two vanish.
Repeated application of the ordinary Fréchet chain rule therefore gives the stated formula. The last
assertion follows because SX includes a single supported slot into X and AY applies Qγ in the chosen
output slot.

4 The partition chain rule and packet decorations

Let U ⊆X and V ⊆Y be open, let G : U →Y and F  : V →Z be Cn, and assume G(U) ⊆V . Fix x ∈U.
Write Πn for set partitions of {1, . . . , n}. Within each block the directions are listed by increasing index.
Blocks may be listed by increasing least element to make every displayed tuple unambiguous.

Theorem 4.1 (Faà di Bruno in Banach spaces). For n ≥1 and h1, . . . , hn ∈X,

           Dn(F ◦G)(x)[h1, . . . , hn] = X D|π|F(Gx) h D|B|G(x)[hi : i ∈B] : B ∈π i .
                                     π∈Πn

The order of blocks is immaterial because Fréchet higher derivatives are symmetric.

Proof. For n = 1 this is the chain rule. Suppose the identity holds at order n and the maps are Cn+1.
Differentiate a summand in direction hn+1. Differentiating the outer D|π|F(Gx) produces the same
partition with the new singleton block {n+1}. Differentiating the argument D|B|G(x)[hi : i ∈B] produces
the partition obtained by adjoining n + 1 to the existing block B. Every partition of {1, . . . , n + 1}
arises in exactly one of these ways, depending on whether {n + 1} is a singleton. The product and chain
rules apply to the bounded multilinear evaluations, and all sums are finite. Induction completes the
proof.

Corollary 4.2 (Decorated packet chain rule). Fix input labels αi, directions hi ∈Xαi, and an output
label δ. For each partition π and intermediate label function γ : π →J, replace the Bth argument of the
outer derivative by Qγ(B)D|B|G(x)[hi : i ∈B]. The sum over all such decorations, followed by Rδ, equals
the δ output packet of Dn(F ◦G)(x)[h1, . . . , hn].

Proof. In every outer argument of Theorem 4.1, insert the identity on Y as Pγ∈J Qγ. Expand by
multilinearity. The output projection Rδ distributes over the finite sum. Because the directions are
already in their actual packet ranges, this is precisely the literal packet-jet expression. No statement
assumes that mixed input labels disappear.

nonzero summands can cancel. For example, take X = Z = R with one packet, Y = R2 with its two
coordinate packets, G(t) = (t, t), and F(y1, y2) = y1 −y2. At order one both decorated terms are nonzero
and their sum is zero. If M = 0, then Y = 0. In that case, for n ≥1 the term count and every derivative

Plate III.1    / CHAPTER III / A WORKED VISUAL COMPANION

 Three objects, three different questions

   Chapter III, mathematical text: Section 1, Section 4, Section 5

  An edge operator moves data between named packets. An exact coordinate change describes the same data
in another complete chart. A connection supplies an additional choice of transport. The three can use similar
arrows while making different mathematical assertions.

    EDGE                  EXACT                CHOSEN
    ACTION               COORDINATES            CONNECTION

                                        (3, 2)
  0   0   0

  2   0   0                                                            (1, 1)

   𝑒0 ⟼2𝑒1         one unchanged ambient vector   𝐻= ( 10 11 ) ≠𝐼

Three actual models used below: a single supported matrix entry, one ambient vector in three coordinate systems, and a shear
obtained as chosen loop transport. The coordinates in the middle are not three different ambient vectors.

  One chapter, three tests

  For an edge word, ask whether the target of each step matches the source of the next. For exact coordinates,
ask whether analysis and synthesis are inverses. For a connection, ask whether its transports through two steps
agree with its declared direct transports. None of these tests can replace another.

  This guide follows explicit integer and rational matrices through these tests. Each example has an inspectable
input, calculation, and conclusion. Vector drawings display those calculations rather than replace them. A graph
with two paths can have zero net transfer. A loop with trace two and determinant one can still differ from the
identity.

  Scope of the worked models

  The worked models illustrate the finite algebraic core. The main text also develops rooted tree expansions, non-
linear defects, obstruction objects, filtered lifting, and analytic transport under their stated hypotheses. Those
ordinary mathematical developments have a wider scope than the finite Lean contract. The present models ex-
plain the finite mechanisms and provide a route into the broader chapter.

  Read this as: Follow the object, not the arrow shape. A typed transfer can vanish, a complete coordinate
   loop must telescope, and an independently chosen connection can have genuine algebraic holonomy.

The board tests all ordered pairs. Columns are the first executed edge and rows are the second. A shaded cell gives the ordered
coefficient of a valid walk. A cross means the product is zero by type mismatch.
  The surviving words are 𝑎𝑐, 𝑏𝑐, 𝑐𝑑, 𝑑𝑎, 𝑑𝑏. Their coefficients are 6, −3, 3, 2, −1, respectively. Their endpoints
determine where these numbers enter the matrix:
                                     0  0  1              0  3  0
                    ⎛    ⎞      ⎛    ⎞                 𝑇= ⎜1  0  0⎟ ,    𝑇2 = ⎜0  0  1⎟ .
                    ⎝0  3  0⎠      ⎝3  0  0⎠

At row 2, column 0, the two parallel choices give 6 −3 = 3. Deduplicating the edge labels before summing
would alter the operator. On the other hand, adding the parallel coefficients in the already assembled matrix is
legitimate: both act in the same supported matrix position.

  The same calculation extends from pairs to all finite words by distributivity. The included check enumerates
every word through length six and independently accumulates the endpoint coefficients. The empty word is
treated separately as the identity.

  Read this as: The matrix power is a signed, ordered walk sum. It is not simply the number of paths, and a
   graph edge is not identified solely by its endpoints.

The formal core and analytic continuation

The formal development combines finite algebraic constructions, exact nonlinear packet coordinates,
and an analytic packet interface. Its verification record includes compilation in the pinned environment,
an audit of the compiled ownership boundary and transitive axioms, replay of the owned logical dec-
larations into an environment initially containing only upstream dependencies, and rejection controls.


The mathematical objects are the actual ranges

The input space for a jet is the dependent finite product of the submodules ran 𝑃𝛼𝑖. The output is
ran 𝑄𝛾. These submodules carry their inherited norms. The continuous jet uses the actual inclusions
and output restriction. Its underlying multilinear map is the previously defined algebraic range jet.

                                      ‖𝐽𝛾∣𝛼𝐵‖ ≤‖𝑄𝛾‖ ‖𝐵‖.

The product of norms of the input projectors belongs to the estimate for the ambient extension. It
is unnecessary in the sharper bound for the literal restricted jet. Closed ranges and the continuous
coordinate equivalence are proved for continuous projectors.


  Source module                    Formal content

  PacketCoordinates.lean               Analysis and synthesis for a finite complete pairwise annihilating
  PacketDirectSum.lean                idempotent family, with range-valued coordinates and the direct-
                              sum comparison.
  NonlinearPacketCoordinates.lean      Exact coordinate representation of arbitrary functions, composi-
                                           tion and coordinate changes.
  MultilinearPacketJets.lean          Complete finite multilinear expansion, literal range jets, and recon-
                                             struction. Mixed input labels are retained.
  BoundedPacketJetNorm.lean          The ambient continuous multilinear extension and its product
                               norm bound.
  ContinuousPacketJets.lean           Closed ranges, continuous packet coordinates, literal continuous
                                       range jets, the sharper norm bound, and specialization to iterat
                                          edFDeriv.
  PacketJetComposition.lean           Composition over all finite ordered partitions and intermediate la-
                                                bels, structural vanishing, and one-way support inclusion.


  All paths in this table are relative to formal/KomorebiPaperIII/. The formal sources state their
own field, norm, finiteness and regularity assumptions. The composition theorem assumes ContDiff
At K n f x and ContDiffAt K n g (f x). The intermediate and output projectors are continuous. Input
range inclusions are continuous without an additional continuity hypothesis on the input family.


What the derivative notation commits to

Mathlib defines iteratedFDeriv as a total function. Reconstructing its chosen value is unconditional.
That identity alone does not assert differentiability of an arbitrary map. The composition theorem
supplies local differentiability hypotheses explicitly. Its OrderedFinpartition n uses the canonical
order of the blocks by their greatest elements. Each original slot is selected by the partition embedding,
and every intermediate label assignment is summed. In the real or complex smooth setting, symmetry
identifies this formula with the manuscript’s unordered-partition notation.

The support theorem says that a nonzero composite jet has at least one decorated partition with
a nonzero outer jet and all inner jets nonzero. It gives no converse. Constituent maps can compose to
zero, and distinct terms can cancel. The formal composition identity also covers order zero through the
unique empty partition. The positive-order manuscript formula requires no new nullary convention.


Compilation and kernel evidence

The verification run compiled 16 production modules from an initially empty owned object directory.
The compiled ownership audit recorded 608 owned declarations. The clean kernel replay accepted
594 logical declarations, with 14 generated runtime helpers separately inventoried. The full build,
ownership audit, kernel replay, and control suite all passed.

  The exact compiler is Lean 4.34.0-rc2, commit 6a10ac8c22beadecabdbb0919c2b50214762f91d.
Mathlib is pinned at aeb72f1e9981b6d35b426b16dca7759be3e7ba06. The machine-readable summary
is formal/verification/FINAL_VERIFICATION_SUMMARY.json. The full command transcripts and
exact source snapshots accompany every phase. The owned audit examines compiled declarations by
module ownership, including names outside the main namespace. It rejects project axioms, unreviewed
opaque or partial declarations, unsafe declarations, and transitive axioms outside the standard basis
propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound.

profiles.text:
How to use this volume

Begin with cyclic projection and the signed differential cycle. The reciprocal sections then build
parameter polynomials, Appell systems, and theta polynomials from a unit series. The second
half follows the same denominator through large zero geometry, canonical products, and zero
zeta functions.
The visual atlas at the end of this chapter supplies twenty-six worked plates. The companion Lean
guide follows the formal declarations and their hypotheses. The main text contains sixty-eight
theorem-like results and ninety-five numbered records.



                                     Overview

       Fix a positive integer 𝑁. Root of unity projection of the exponential produces residue-class
   sections that, for 𝜆≠0, form a basis for 𝑦(𝑁) = 𝜆𝑁𝑦. The signed sections for 𝑦(𝑁) = −𝑦yield
   the denominator D𝑁and its reduced form Δ𝑁. We derive reciprocal coefficient polynomials, Bell
   and Newton recurrences, an additive parameter law, and residue section Appell and theta families.
   For 𝑁≥2, Δ𝑁has order 1/𝑁. We specialize classical two term zero theory for exponential sums to
   the regular exponent polygon. In this equal-weight family, conjugation symmetry combined with
   unique near-model localization places all sufficiently large zeros exactly on the symmetry rays,
   and direct expansion gives their leading displacement and derivative sign. The classical perimeter
   law yields zero-counting asymptotics with explicit leading constants and bounded error. These
    results give genus-zero products, the standard diagonal Fredholm representation, zero-power-sum
   formulas for reciprocal and logarithmic coefficients, nearest-zero coefficient asymptotics, and
   meromorphic continuation of the symmetry-orbit zero zeta by comparison with the Hurwitz
   zeta function. Complex powers are interpreted either formally or through a fixed logarithm on
   a zero-free domain. This chapter treats only this cyclic analytic family. Arithmetic interpolation,
   general nonlinear trees, general resolvent theory, and abstract completion are reserved for Chapters
    IX, III, VI, and X.


Formal scope and evidence

The recorded formal contract covers all sixty-eight theorem-like manuscript results under their
stated hypotheses. The formalization ledger identifies the corresponding declarations.
Imported standard fact 11.1 is used in the ordinary manuscript growth argument. The Lean
growth-order proofs establish that step separately. Open questions, branch choices, multiplicities,
and the hypotheses of coefficient asymptotics remain explicit. Finite computations support the
worked models. The companion Lean guide records the replay using pinned sources, declaration-
kind checks, axiom audit, and their limits.

1 Introduction

For a power series
                                    𝐹(𝑧) = ∑ 𝑎𝑚𝑧𝑚
                                        𝑚≥0

and a positive integer 𝑁, the coefficients may be separated according to the residue of 𝑚modulo
𝑁. Root of unity averaging gives exact projection operators for this separation. This elementary
construction is usually called a multisection or a root filter. It appears throughout the classical theory of
generating functions and special functions. Background on multisections, hypergeometric functions,
and related coefficient systems may be found in [Rai60, AAR99, Com74].

  Chapters I and II developed typed seed grammars, exact projector packets, and finite residue-
projector algebra, while Chapter III treated typed edge operators and exact coordinate transport [P.26a,
P.26b, P.26c]. The root filter used below is the finite cyclic scalar specialization of that earlier projector
calculus. The signed companion matrix is likewise a concrete cyclic instance, not a replacement for
Chapter III’s general typed-edge theory.

  This chapter follows the consequences of applying the cyclic projections to the exponential function.
The projected exponentials form a finite differential system. After one sign is inserted around the
derivative cycle, they form a basis for
                                              𝑦(𝑁) = −𝑦.

The section with initial value one is
                               D𝑁(𝑧) = ∑ (−1)𝑛𝑧𝑁𝑛                                                   (𝑁𝑛)!.                                           𝑛≥0

Its reciprocal powers produce polynomial coefficient families. Its logarithmic derivative produces a
scalar higher Riccati identity. The same reciprocal construction applied to every exponential section
gives normalized residue section functions and ordinary Appell polynomial sequences. These cyclic
exponential sections and their matrix addition laws belong to the generalized hyperbolic function
literature [Sch92, Mul05]. Appell and binomial-type sequences are discussed in [Rom84, Com74].
  The second half of this chapter concerns the zeros of D𝑁. The finite exponential sum

                                            1
                                 D𝑁(𝑧) = ∑  𝑒𝜂𝑧                           𝑁
                                              𝜂𝑁=−1

has a regular polygon of exponents. The general relation between an exponent polygon and the zero
strips of an exponential sum goes back to Pólya and Langer. Later developments include the work of
Moreno and the treatment in Levin’s monograph [Pól20, Lan31, Mor73, Lev80]. Bleher and Mallison
give a particularly close general result: for convex-polygon exponential sums they locate all sufficiently
large zeros in two term strips and prove exponential localization and simplicity [BM06]. The regular
polygon and conjugation symmetry of the present family specialize that theory to 𝑁exact rays. We
give a self-contained specialization because its notation is used throughout the product and zeta theory,
and we compute the leading displacement term for this family. The resulting counting formulas have
explicit leading constants and bounded error.

For 𝑁≥2, the order of Δ𝑁is 1/𝑁. Its Hadamard product therefore has genus zero. The logarithm of
this product identifies the transfer tangent coefficients with power sums of the reduced zeros. The large
zero formula also compares the reduced zero zeta with a Hurwitz zeta function. Standard material on
entire functions, canonical products, and exponential sums appears in [Boa54, Lev80, Tit39]. We use
singularity analysis in the form described in [FS09] and the classical continuation of the Hurwitz zeta
function from [Apo76].

  The cyclic exponential sections and their matrix addition laws have a classical literature. The tools
used below include Appell and binomial-type sequences, canonical products, singularity analysis,
and Fredholm determinants. These tools are also standard. Our aim is to organize this symmetric
specialization and link its reciprocal coefficients to reduced-zero data. No historical priority is asserted
for the component constructions.

  The central idea

  The same object is read in different coordinates. Selecting residues makes its Taylor coefficients
   visible. A signed shift makes the differential system finite. Passing to 𝑤= 𝑧𝑁removes rotational

the rotational symmetry. The reduced variable

function of 𝑤.

PLATE IV.1 / READER'S GUIDE

A coefficient can become zero data

Chapter IV: Section 2, Section 7, Section 11, Section 12.

This guide follows a concrete analytic family through three descriptions: selected Taylor coefficients, a finite
differential system, and the zeros of an entire function. The formulas are linked, but the evidence needed for
each description is different.

    COEFFICIENT LANES    RECIPROCAL COEFFICIENTS       ZERO ORBITS


     𝑧0    𝑧3    𝑧6    𝑧9                                 1    0    0

     𝑧1    𝑧4    𝑧7   𝑧10                         −1                                          2   1    0
     𝑧2    𝑧5    𝑧8   𝑧11
                                         1  −1                                         24                                                2   1

    𝑚≡𝑗(mod 3)                1,   12,   24,5 …               {𝜌, 𝑖𝜌, −𝜌, −𝑖𝜌}

Keep three small models in view
For 𝑁= 2, the signed denominator is 𝐷2(𝑧) = cos 𝑧. Its reciprocal is the familiar secant series. For 𝑁= 3, a
third exponential perturbs the zeros of a dominant cosine. For 𝑁= 4, an exact factorization gives a complete
zero picture:                             √     √
                                  𝐷4(𝑧) = cos(𝑧/  2) cosh(𝑧/  2).

The examples move between these orders deliberately. Order two makes the coefficient arithmetic transparent.
Order three shows a genuine displacement. Order four makes orbit reduction completely explicit.

Three routes through the guide

Route               Pages and question

Algebra first          Plates IV.3–IV.16: selection, signs, reciprocals, and finite differential operators.

A root filter is an exact vote

Chapter IV: Theorem 3.1, Proposition 3.2.

For 𝑁= 4, write 𝜔= 𝑖. To extract residue 𝑗, evaluate the function at four rotated arguments and attach the phase
𝑖−𝑗ℓ:
                                                1  3

                                                          ℓ=0

A monomial 𝑎𝑚𝑧𝑚is multiplied by the finite average of 𝑖(𝑚−𝑗)ℓ. Matching phases all vote 1. Nonmatching phases
cancel exactly.

             −𝑖

An example that can be checked coefficient by coefficient

Take 𝐹(𝑧) = ∑ 𝑚=0(𝑚+ 1)𝑧𝑚. Then
                              ℬ4,2𝐹= 3𝑧2 + 7𝑧6 + 11𝑧10.

Applying the same selector again changes nothing. Applying a different selector gives zero. Summing the four
selected polynomials returns the original 𝐹.

Selection is also a symmetry condition
For the selected polynomial 𝐹2, rotation gives 𝐹2(𝑖𝑧) = −𝐹2(𝑧). More generally, a residue-𝑗section satisfies
𝐹𝑗(𝜔𝑧) = 𝜔𝑗𝐹𝑗(𝑧). The phase label therefore describes both the coefficient addresses and the response to rotation.

PLATE IV.4  / CYCLIC CONVOLUTION

Products mix the residue lanes

Chapter IV: Theorem 3.3.

Selection separates a function additively. It does not make multiplication diagonal. A residue-𝑖term multiplied
by a residue-𝑗term lands in residue 𝑖+ 𝑗(mod 𝑁). For 𝑁= 3, use

                𝐹= 1 + 2𝑧+ 3𝑧2 + 𝑧3,  𝐺= 2 + 𝑧+ 𝑧2.

The table displays every product of their three selected sections.
                  2               𝑧               𝑧2

   𝑧3 + 1       2𝑧3 + 2          𝑧4 + 𝑧          𝑧5 + 𝑧2

       2𝑧         4𝑧              2𝑧2             2𝑧3

      3𝑧2         6𝑧2             3𝑧3             3𝑧4


                      ℬ3,0(𝐹𝐺) = 2 + 7𝑧3

          shaded cells: (0, 0), (1, 2), (2, 1) all land in residue 0


The shaded cells contribute to residue zero:

                                  2(1 + 𝑧3) + (2𝑧)(𝑧2) + (3𝑧2)𝑧= 2 + 7𝑧3.

Keeping only the product of the residue-zero inputs would give 2 + 2𝑧3 and lose five units of the 𝑧3 coefficient.
The mixed cells are part of the exact result.

The general rule

                            ℬ𝑁,𝑘(𝐹𝐺) = ∑  (ℬ𝑁,𝑖𝐹)(ℬ𝑁,𝑗𝐺).
                                                𝑖+𝑗≡𝑘(𝑁)

Every pair belongs to exactly one output residue. No term is discarded and no coefficient is estimated. This finite
cyclic convolution is the algebra behind the later addition formulas and block-coefficient recurrences.

   vanish.

1 How to read this formalization

1.1 What has been completed

Chapter IV studies one scalar cyclic family through several realizations. A residue-class projector se-
lects coefficients. Its exponential sections become entire functions. Signed sections produce a distin-
guished denominator, whose reciprocal coefficients form parameterized polynomial families. The de-
nominator’s zeros then control canonical products, a diagonal determinant, coefficient asymptotics,
and zeta functions.

  The formal development follows these transitions explicitly. It does not identify a formal series with
an analytic function by notation alone. It proves summation bridges, matches ordinary and factorial-
normalized coefficients, and carries zero multiplicities and logarithm choices into the analytic state-
ments.

  The completed formal contract has 68 full scoped manuscript results, zero partial, and zero un-
mapped. The 151 map rows name 1,164 distinct declarations: 953 theorems and 211 constructions. The
saved fail-closed namespace audit reports 2,234 declarations, including 1,999 theorem declarations.
These are different counts. The namespace includes supporting material beyond the explicit map, while
the map includes definitions as well as theorems. Neither is a count of independent mathematical dis-
coveries.


1.2 Formal verification and source reconciliation



    Evidence                   Verified scope

    Formal execution         The source contract is supported by the preserved aggregate build, 43 se-
                            mantic checks, exact target-kind resolution, and kernel audit. The verifica-
                                 tion chapter records the separate replay using pinned sources for all 118
                             production modules.
     Static reconciliation        This guide checks source checksums, exact map and contract parity, lexical
                              source locations, target sets in the audit source and saved transcript, depen-
                           dency pins, and excerpt identity.


  The transcript permits only the disclosed standard transitive axioms propext, Classical.choice,
and Quot.sound. This is a claim about the audited Lean environment and its declarations, not an asser-
tion of assumption-free mathematics. Hypotheses appear in declaration types and remain part of each
theorem.

  This ordering is a reading route, not the exact import order. The final nine modules close 15 pre-

statements to the analytic or literal displayed forms requested by the manuscript.


1.4 Reading a Lean declaration

An expression such as (hN : 0 < N) is an explicit hypothesis. Braces indicate implicit arguments whose
values Lean may infer. They do not erase hypotheses. A proposition such as HasSum f x asserts con-
vergence of the indexed sum to the displayed value. A bare tsum is an operation with a total definition
and does not, by itself, assert that a series converges. The same distinction applies to Multipliable and
an infinite product.

  Formal power series, polynomials, complex functions, and continuous linear maps inhabit different
types. The transition between them is usually the mathematically important theorem. In this guide, a
short final proof often rests on substantial earlier modules. A proof of the final Hadamard identity in
two lines is not the whole product argument.

  The code excerpts are literal source intervals, including their proofs. They are reading excerpts inside
the original module context, not independent files that can be pasted without imports, variables, names-
pace declarations, or local instances. The complete source is supplied. The excerpt manifest records
each original file, line interval, file hash, excerpt hash, and display hash.


1.5 Boundaries that completion preserves

Imported standard fact 11.1 remains imported and is outside the 68-result contract. The checked order
proofs do not need it. The work does not claim universal simplicity of all zeros, positivity of every
reduced zero, a full displacement expansion, or a zeta functional equation. Eventual simplicity and
exact asymptotic statements are proved with their stated ranges. Nearest-pole results keep their integer
reciprocal-order and local pole hypotheses. Complex powers use a formal series, a normalized germ,
or one fixed holomorphic logarithm on the stated domain.

  Chapter IV’s diagonal determinant is a concrete scalar-family specialization. It is not the general
bounded-operator theory allocated to Chapter VI, the arithmetic interpolation theory of Chapter IX, or
the abstract completion questions of Chapter X.

 Failures and repairs
 Warning policy

 The inherited -E warning setting accepted an isolated deliberately admitted proof with exit code 0. The
 corrected -DwarningAsError=true setting rejected the same fixture with exit code 1. The active replay
 uses the corrected policy. The production source files were not weakened or edited.

 Startup race in a control fixture

 The first new verifier suite passed 37 of 38 tests. Its descendant-cleanup test timed out before the parent
 announced startup, so it did not establish that a descendant had started. The repaired fixture waits for explicit
 child readiness, then applies a separate bounded execution deadline. The final 42-test suite passes. The failed
  first run remains in the archive.

 Distribution and availability metadata

 The old 908-row distribution manifest still listed 73 excluded font files. Its verifier therefore failed. The
 recovered 836-file tree is preserved and a new top-level manifest records the actual distribution. No fonts were
 restored. The older available-check runner also described installed symbolic tools as unavailable. The new
 runner reports actual dependencies and executes the underlying suites.

 What could not be recovered

 The exact earlier unsaved fixture-control failure was not recovered. This release does not claim to reproduce
 that absent script. Instead, it directly exercises the recovered checker API using its actual typed records, and
 records new compilation, audit and control evidence. An initial network-based runtime recovery was
 unavailable in this container. The archived offline runtime supplied the successful pinned compiler and cache.

  Failures are preserved as failures. Successful replacement checks have their own source fingerprints and receipts. No licence
 was selected or changed.

How to use this volume

   Part I. The twenty-result formal core develops exact polyphase reconstruction, filter transfers,
   Hilbert packet operators, finite adaptive trees, edge error bounds, and Smith coordinates.

   Part II. The complete extended development treats lattice coordinates, stable banks, singular pack-
   ets, separated jump recovery, geometric error bounds, and multiscale localization.

  Visual atlas. Forty worked plates close the volume. The separate visual guide provides the same
  examples, and the Lean guide gives the precise formal contract.



Reading this chapter

This chapter develops signal calculus in two complementary parts. Part I gives twenty results on exact
coordinates, filtering, adaptive selection and packet error. Part II develops lattice coordinates, stable
banks, singular packets and separated jump recovery, with E-prefixed section numbers. The two parts
share constructions but use them under different hypotheses.

  For a first reading, follow Part I Sections 1–7. These sections establish the coordinate maps, filter trans-
fers, exact reconstruction, and the separation of packet error from smooth approximation error. Section
11 develops finite adaptive selection. Sections 13–14 give the cyclic Smith realization. Continue with
Part II Sections E2–E6 for lattice and stability generalizations, E7–E11 for singular packets and recov-
ery, and E12–E14 for nonlinear and Cayley coordinates. Each visual plate identifies the corresponding
manuscript result.

  The formal companion maps all twenty Part I results to 225 supporting Lean theorem targets across
23 proof modules. Part II has ordinary written proofs and is outside that twenty-result formal map.
Exact examples and numerical studies have their own stated scopes. The formal companion and source
records distinguish kernel verification, finite checks and numerical replay.

  The two broad edge recovery conjectures remain open. Part II proves recovery for a declared one-
dimensional separated jump class under its sampling, contrast, and noise assumptions. These results
do not supply universal image segmentation or infinite-tree consistency. Numerical illustrations keep
the finite interpretation stated in their captions.

profiles.text:
Part I: The formal core




   Coordinates first, decisions second

 A residue decomposition changes the coordinates of a signal without changing its information.
   Filtering then acts between those coordinates. Approximation enters when an operator compresses
  a component or when a decision discards coefficients. The formal core follows these operations in
   that order.


                                       Overview

         This chapter develops the signal realization of the projector-resolved seed calculus. The impulse
      𝛿0 is taken as a primitive signal seed and its shift orbit supplies the address system. Residue pro-
       jectors split a sequence into exact polyphase channels, nested divisibility gives exact refinement,
     and every finite impulse-response operator becomes a matrix of packet transfers. The standard
      perfect-reconstruction condition for a filter bank is therefore an analysis–synthesis identity in the
    common operator language of the series. Haar analysis and every finite-depth wavelet-packet trans-
     form are treated on complex ℓ2, together with concrete finite-signal models and a predict–update
       lifting step. The edge problem is separated into two statements. When a discontinuity packet is
    known and retained exactly, approximation error is exactly the approximation error of the remain-
      ing smooth packet. No spectral approximation of the jump is performed. When the packet is esti-
      mated, a symmetric-difference bound isolates mask error, amplitude error, and smooth-background
       error. Numerical studies compare global Fourier truncation, exact known-packet reconstruction,
     and a deliberately narrow positive-contrast estimator in one and two dimensions, including curved
      boundaries, corners, and multiple amplitudes. The same cyclic phase action is then placed on the
     Smith reflection disk. Its pullback through the Cayley transform is a Möbius action on impedance,
     and the two-phase case is precisely impedance–admittance inversion. Nonlinear coefficient prod-
      ucts obey cyclic packet convolution. The accompanying formal development gives a Lean formal-
      ization of all twenty theorem-like statements under the hypotheses stated below: 225 supporting
     theorem targets in 23 modules. Eighteen regenerated figures, machine-readable numerical results,
      the 33-test original companion suite, and 36 additional exact-model and verifier tests accompany
      the chapter. Exact signal theorems, limited numerical estimators, classical constructions, and open
      recovery problems are kept distinct throughout.


  Scope and claim boundary

  The chapter proves exact polyphase reconstruction, exact finite filter-transfer identities, perfect
   reconstruction for the stated filter banks, the conditional known-edge theorem, mask and ampli-
  tude perturbation bounds, nonlinear residue-convolution laws, and the Smith-coordinate phase
   action. It does not claim that every discontinuity can be detected automatically, that every form
   of Gibbs ringing has been eliminated, or that the supplied two-class estimator is a universal seg-
  mentation method. The estimator is included as one reproducible finite example. For every finite
  packet refinement tree, the chapter proves existence of a globally optimal complete pruning, an
   exact dynamic-programming selector for additive costs, and a deterministic margin-stability cer-
   tificate. Wavelets, filter banks, the Cayley transform, and the classical Smith grid are treated as
   classical inputs organized in the common seed–packet–refinement language.

Plate V.1    / PAPER V / A WORKED VISUAL COMPANION

Three objects, three different questions

Chapter V: Section 1, Section 6, Section 11, Section 13.

A packet calculus can reorganize a signal exactly, choose among finitely many representations, or describe a
nonlinear coordinate geometry. These are not the same task. This guide keeps one concrete object in view for
each, so that the reader can compute rather than only follow arrows.

    SIGNAL COORDINATES        FINITE TREE CHOICES        REFLECTION ORBIT


                                       ∅

                                 0          1

                              00    01  100 101  11


    𝑓= 𝑠+ 𝑗   in ℚ16         26 complete prunings          Γ = 12𝑖𝑘

A signal that can be checked by hand
Our main finite signal is 𝑓= 𝑠+ 𝑗∈ℚ16. The background repeats
                                             4(0,1    1, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2, −1),
and 𝑗[𝑛] = 3 at 6 ≤𝑛< 12, with 𝑗[𝑛] = 0 elsewhere. This is a discrete background model, not an assertion of
continuum smoothness. Its energy is exactly 57. We use it for residue coordinates, Haar transforms, coefficient
deletion, and known-packet cancellation.

A tree whose alternatives can all be seen
The full binary tree of depth three has only 26 complete prunings. We enumerate all of them, compute a unique
mixed-depth optimum, and certify its stability with rational costs. The displayed objective is deliberately explicit,
not claimed to be a universal score for signal quality.

A coordinate orbit with no hidden numerical poles
The four reflection points Γ = 𝑖𝑘/2 map to four exact impedances. A second orbit passes through infinity. Ho-
mogeneous coordinates make that point an ordinary part of the construction.

   Read this as: Exact coordinates preserve information. An optimizer chooses coordinates. An estimator
   must still identify information not already supplied.
